strand.introHeading: Ratio, proportion and rates of change
strand.metaDescription: GCSE ratio, proportion and rates of change: ratio, proportion, percentage change, compound measures, growth and decay.

topics.title: Ratio
topics.cardDescription: Ratio notation, dividing in a ratio, combining ratios, maps and similar shapes.
topics.metaDescription: GCSE ratio: notation and simplifying, dividing quantities in a ratio, combining ratios, scale drawings, maps and similar shapes, with worked examples throughout.

subtopics.title: Ratio notation
subtopics.description: Recording comparisons with the colon, why order matters, and three-part ratios.
subtopics.coverNote: Introduce the colon notation a : b and a : b : c, order mattering, writing ratios from counts, words and bar models, and reading comparisons aloud. Whole-number parts only; simplifying belongs to simplifying-ratios, converting to fractions of the whole to fractions-of-the-whole, and part:whole distinctions to their sibling page. Both tiers. (R4)

subtopics.title: Simplifying a ratio
subtopics.description: Dividing every part by the same factor, so 12 : 18 becomes 2 : 3.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover simplifying two- and three-part whole-number ratios by common factors or the HCF in one step, recognising equivalent ratios, and simplest-form checks. Integer parts in and out; mixed units are ratios-with-units, decimal 1 : n forms are one-to-n-ratios, and HCF technique itself is taught in Number. Both tiers. (R4)

subtopics.title: Ratios with mixed units
subtopics.description: Converting to the same unit before simplifying, and why the ratio is unitless.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover converting both quantities to a common unit (mm, cm, m; g, kg; minutes, hours; pence, pounds) before simplifying, choosing the smaller unit, and why the finished ratio is unitless. Everyday metric and time conversions only, assumed from Number's measures pages. Rates comparing unlike quantities live under Compound measures. Both tiers. (R4, R1)

subtopics.title: Writing a ratio in the form 1 : n
subtopics.description: Dividing both parts by one of them so scales and mixtures compare directly.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover rewriting any ratio as 1 : n or n : 1 by dividing through, n decimal or fractional, calculator and non-calculator, and using the form to compare scales, mixtures and strengths directly. Interpreting 1 : n map scales in context belongs to map-scales; this page owns the rewriting technique. Both tiers. (R4, R6)

subtopics.title: Part:part and part:whole ratios
subtopics.description: Telling the two kinds of ratio apart, and converting each into the other.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover distinguishing part:part from part:whole statements, converting each to the other in two- and three-part cases, and decoding wordings like 'one in five' or '2 boys for every 3 girls'. Sharing a quantity given either form is dividing-in-a-ratio; writing parts as fractions is fractions-of-the-whole. Both tiers. (R5)

subtopics.title: From a ratio to fractions of the whole
subtopics.description: Reading the fraction of the whole each part represents, and working back.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover reading fractions of the whole from a : b and a : b : c (2 : 3 gives 2/5 and 3/5, never 2/3), rebuilding a ratio from given fractions, and one part as a fraction of another. This page owns N11's fraction-in-ratio work; fraction arithmetic itself stays in Number. Both tiers. (R8, N11)

subtopics.title: Dividing a quantity in a ratio
subtopics.description: Sharing an amount in a given ratio by finding the value of one part first.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover sharing an amount in two- and three-part ratios by valuing one part, plus the part:whole route via fractions, money, mass and length contexts, calculator and non-calculator, with an adding-back check. Reverse cases from one share or a difference are the sibling pages; percentage shares stay with Percentage change. Both tiers. (R5)

subtopics.title: Finding the whole from one share
subtopics.description: Recovering the total and the other shares when only one part's value is given.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover recovering one part's value, the total and every other share when a single share is given, two- and three-part ratios, including 'Amy gets 40 pounds; how much does Ben get?' phrasing. Warn against dividing the known share by the total parts. Difference-given problems are the sibling page. Both tiers. (R5)

subtopics.title: Sharing when the difference is given
subtopics.description: Finding one part from the difference between shares, then rebuilding the total.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover sharing problems that state the difference between two shares: divide the difference by the difference in parts, value one part, rebuild all shares and the total. Include three-part ratios and money or age contexts. Total-given sharing is dividing-in-a-ratio; ratios that change after an event are changing-the-ratio. Both tiers. (R5)

subtopics.title: Writing a division as a ratio
subtopics.description: Turning stated amounts back into a ratio in simplest form, in the order named.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover writing stated amounts as a ratio in the order named and simplifying, including from a total and one share (subtract first) and from fractions or percentages of the whole. Match units before writing, per ratios-with-units. Two and three parts only; this delivers R5's express-a-division clause. Both tiers. (R5)

subtopics.title: Mixing and concentration problems
subtopics.description: Ratios in paint mixes and concentrations, and comparing mixture strengths.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover paint, mortar, squash and alloy mixtures: scaling a mix, finding one ingredient from another, comparing strengths via unit fractions or 1 : n, and limited-ingredient maxima. Deciding same-strength is the key question type. Density of a mixture sits under Compound measures; serving-based recipes are Proportion's scaling-a-recipe. Both tiers. (R5)

subtopics.title: When the ratio changes
subtopics.description: Ratio-change problems solved by pinning down the part that stays fixed.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover problems where adding, removing or transferring quantity changes the ratio: pin the unchanged quantity, or set shares as multiples of x and solve a linear equation. Two-part ratios mainly. Examined at both tiers, but the algebraic route is crossover-to-Higher demand; equation-solving technique itself belongs to Algebra. (R5)

subtopics.title: A ratio as a multiplier
subtopics.description: The multiplicative link between two quantities as a fraction or multiplier.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover expressing one quantity as a fraction or multiplier of another from their ratio, fractions below and above 1 both required, and using the multiplier both ways to find either quantity. Include 'B is 3/2 of A' language. Fractions of the whole are the sibling page; percentage comparison lives under Percentage change. Both tiers. (R3, R6)

subtopics.title: Combining two ratios
subtopics.description: Merging a : b and b : c into a three-part ratio by matching the shared part.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover merging a : b and b : c into a : b : c by scaling both to a common value of the shared part (LCM), then answering sharing or comparison questions from the result. Include three-person money problems and chained exchange rates. Two given ratios only; proportionality equations belong to Proportion. Both tiers. (R5, R4)

subtopics.title: Ratios and linear functions
subtopics.description: Why quantities in a fixed ratio obey y = kx, and the ratio in the gradient.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover why a fixed ratio y : x means y = kx, plotting ratio pairs as a straight line through the origin, reading the ratio from the gradient, and translating between ratio, fraction and function statements. Gradient mechanics and equations of lines are Algebra's; general proportion graphs are Proportion's direct-proportion-graphs. Both tiers. (R8, R14)

subtopics.title: Scale factors
subtopics.description: The multiplier from object lengths to image lengths, and back by dividing.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover the scale factor between an object and its image: finding it from one matched pair of lengths, applying it forwards, dividing to reverse, and fractional factors for reductions. Lengths only. Area and volume factors are the Higher similar-shapes pages; enlargement as a transformation with a centre is Geometry's. Both tiers. (R2, R12)

subtopics.title: Scale drawings
subtopics.description: Using a stated scale such as 1 cm to 2 m to link drawing and real object.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover word scales like '1 cm represents 2 m': converting drawing lengths to real lengths and back, measuring a drawing then converting, producing simple scale drawings, and choosing a sensible scale. Ratio-form scales such as 1 : 25 000 belong to map-scales; bearings and accurate constructions are Geometry's. Both tiers. (R2)

subtopics.title: Map scales
subtopics.description: Ratio scales such as 1 : 25 000, converting between map and ground distance.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover unitless ratio scales like 1 : 25 000: map to ground distance and back through the cm-to-km chain, writing a scale as 1 : n from a matched pair of distances, and comparing map scales. Straight-line distances only; routes with bearings sit in Geometry, and word scales are scale-drawings. Both tiers. (R2, R1)

subtopics.title: Lengths in similar shapes
subtopics.description: Finding missing lengths with the length factor from any corresponding pair.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover missing lengths in similar shapes and triangles using the length scale factor or equal ratios of corresponding sides, enlargements and reductions, including matched sides in overlapping-triangle diagrams. Establishing similarity and angle arguments belong to Geometry; area and volume factors are the Higher sibling pages, kept out for Foundation's sake. Both tiers. (R12, G19)

subtopics.title: Areas of similar shapes
subtopics.description: Why the area scale factor is the square of the length factor, shown by tiling.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, per the braces on areas in G19. Cover the area factor as the square of the length factor, used both ways: scale an area, or square-root an area ratio to recover the length factor. Include surface areas of similar solids. Lengths stay on the both-tier sibling page; volumes are next door. (R12, G19)

subtopics.title: Volumes of similar shapes
subtopics.description: Why the volume scale factor is the cube of the length factor, used both ways.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, per the braces on volumes in G19. Cover the volume factor as the cube of the length factor, applied to volumes, capacities and masses of similar solids in both directions, including cube-rooting a volume ratio. Mass via density links to Compound measures; switching between area and volume factors is choosing-the-scale-factor. (R12, G19)

subtopics.title: Choosing the right scale factor
subtopics.description: Moving between length, area and volume factors by roots and powers.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only. Cover converting between length, area and volume factors by squaring, cubing and rooting: from any one given ratio find the others, including area-to-volume via the length factor, with fractional and surd answers. Confront the applying-the-length-factor-everywhere error head on. Similarity proofs and trigonometric links stay in Geometry. (R12, G19)

topics.title: Proportion
topics.cardDescription: Direct and inverse proportion, best buys, and the graphs and equations of both.
topics.metaDescription: GCSE proportion: direct and inverse proportion, the unitary method, recipes and best buys, and the graphs and equations of proportionality.

subtopics.title: Proportion as equality of ratios
subtopics.description: Two pairs of quantities are in proportion when their ratios are equal.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover the definition that pairs of quantities are proportional when their ratios are equal: test tables by comparing ratios or unit values, and find a missing value by equating two ratios, cross-multiplication kept informal. Applications go to the unitary-method and sibling pages; the y = kx formalisation waits for later pages. Both tiers. (R7)

subtopics.title: Direct proportion
subtopics.description: Direct proportion: multiply one quantity and the other multiplies the same way.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover the meaning of direct proportion, multiplying one quantity multiplies the other by the same factor, with scaling-factor solutions for cost, mass and length problems and 'is directly proportional to' language. Stress constant ratio, not merely both increasing. The unitary method, graphs and y = kx each get their own page. Both tiers. (R10, R7)

subtopics.title: The unitary method
subtopics.description: Finding the value of one unit first, then scaling up to any number of units.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover finding one unit's value then scaling: cost per item, exchange-rate style conversions, time for one machine, choosing between unitary and scaling-factor routes, calculator and non-calculator. Conversion here means proportional quantities; single measurement units are Number's. Recipes and best buys apply this on the sibling pages. Both tiers. (R10, R5)

subtopics.title: Scaling a recipe
subtopics.description: Scaling every ingredient by the same factor, and serving-size questions.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover scaling ingredient lists by integer, fractional and decimal factors such as 1.5 or 2/3, converting between serving counts both ways, and how-many-can-be-made questions limited by one ingredient. Fraction arithmetic assumed from Number. Value comparison is best-buy-comparisons; mixtures stated as ratios are Ratio's mixing-and-concentrations. Both tiers. (R5, R10)

subtopics.title: Best-buy comparisons
subtopics.description: Comparing value by the price of one unit or the amount one penny buys.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover comparing value across pack sizes by price per unit or amount per penny, three or more packs, and multibuy offers like three-for-two or 25% extra free, with working and units shown. Unit pricing as a bare rate also lives under Compound measures; percentage discounts draw on Percentage change. Both tiers. (R10, R11)

subtopics.title: Inverse proportion
subtopics.description: Inverse proportion: multiply one, and the other divides by the same factor.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover the meaning of inverse proportion, one quantity multiplies and the other divides by the same factor so the product is constant, with 'is inversely proportional to' language and the equivalence to proportionality to 1/x stated informally. Worked contexts are the sibling problems page; constructing y = k/x is Higher's inverse-proportion-equations. Both tiers. (R10, R13)

subtopics.title: Inverse proportion problems
subtopics.description: Workers and time, speed and journey time, solved by finding the fixed product.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover workers and time, taps filling tanks, speed and journey time, and supplies lasting fewer days, all solved via the fixed product such as total worker-hours, including non-integer answers and whole-worker sense checks. Recognising which model applies is the sibling page; algebraic k/x equations are Higher only. Both tiers. (R10)

subtopics.title: Recognising the type of proportion
subtopics.description: Deciding from a table whether a relationship is direct, inverse or neither.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover deciding direct, inverse or neither from a table (test constant ratio or constant product), a graph or a description, with written justification; both columns increasing is not evidence, and y = kx + c is neither. Graph shapes have their own pages; equation construction is Higher. Both tiers. (R10, R14)

subtopics.title: The graph of direct proportion
subtopics.description: A line through the origin, and why one that misses it is not direct proportion.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover the straight line through the origin as direct proportion's signature: recognising it, rejecting lines with a non-zero intercept, reading values both ways, and interpreting the gradient as the unit rate or constant of proportionality. Plotting mechanics are Algebra's; conversion graphs and gradient-as-a-rate build on this page. Both tiers. (R10, R14)

subtopics.title: The graph of inverse proportion
subtopics.description: The reciprocal curve, approaching each axis without ever reaching it.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover recognising the reciprocal curve of inverse proportion, reading values from it both ways, and its behaviour: constant product of coordinates, approaching but never touching either axis, asymptote language kept informal. Recognition and reading only; plotting y = 1/x is Algebra's reciprocal-graphs work, and constructing y = k/x is Higher's sibling page. Both tiers. (R10, R14)

subtopics.title: Conversion graphs
subtopics.description: Reading a conversion graph in both directions, and extending it with the rate.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover reading straight-line conversion graphs, currency, units and temperature, in both directions, drawing one from a rate or two points, and converting amounts beyond the plotted range by using the rate. Include non-origin lines like fixed-charge tariffs. Unit conversion arithmetic is Number's; gradient-as-a-rate under Compound measures continues the idea. Both tiers. (R1, R14)

subtopics.title: Constructing y = kx
subtopics.description: Finding k from one pair of values, then using the equation in both directions.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, from R13's braced 'construct and'. Cover forming y = kx from a proportionality statement plus one value pair, finding k, interpreting it in context, and evaluating either variable. Include statements from words. Foundation meets interpretation on ratios-and-linear-functions and the graph pages; powers and roots follow on proportion-to-powers. (R13, R10)

subtopics.title: Constructing y = k/x
subtopics.description: Writing inverse proportion as y = k/x, since it means proportional to 1/x.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, from R13's braced 'construct and'. Cover forming y = k/x from an inverse statement and one value pair, using the equivalence with proportionality to 1/x, evaluating both ways, and contrasting with the direct case. Curve recognition stays on the both-tier graphs page; squared-denominator forms belong to proportion-to-powers. (R13, R10)

subtopics.title: Proportion to squares, cubes and roots
subtopics.description: Relationships like y = kx² and y = k/x², and finding k when the power is stated.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only. Cover y = kx squared, cubed, square-rooted and k over x squared: form the equation from a statement naming the power plus one value pair, find k, evaluate both directions, and match tables or descriptions to the right form. Powers are always stated, never deduced from data; exponential models live in Growth and decay. (R10, R13)

topics.title: Percentage change
topics.cardDescription: Multipliers, comparing change, reverse percentages, and repeated interest.
topics.metaDescription: GCSE percentage change: multipliers for increase and decrease, profit and loss, reverse percentages, simple interest and repeated change.

subtopics.title: Increase and decrease without a calculator
subtopics.description: Building the change from 50%, 10% and 1%, then adding it on or taking it off.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover non-calculator increase and decrease built from 50%, 10%, 5% and 1% blocks, added on or taken off, with money and measure contexts and estimation checks. Plain percentage-of-an-amount and percentages as parts per hundred are Number's FDP pages, deliberately duplicated territory; the multiplier method follows on the sibling pages. Both tiers. (R9)

subtopics.title: The multiplier for an increase
subtopics.description: Adding the percentage to 100% as a decimal, so a 12% rise becomes ×1.12.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover forming an increase multiplier by adding to 100% and writing as a decimal: 12% gives x1.12, 4.5% gives x1.045, a 150% rise gives x2.5, applied in one calculator step. Percentages above 100% included. Decreases and decoding multipliers are the sibling pages; repeated application waits for repeated-change. Both tiers. (R9)

subtopics.title: The multiplier for a decrease
subtopics.description: Subtracting the percentage from 100%, so a 15% fall becomes ×0.85, not ×0.15.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover forming a decrease multiplier by subtracting from 100%, so 15% off gives x0.85, applying it in one step, and killing the x0.15 error explicitly. Include small decimal rates like 2.5%. Increases are the sibling page; dividing by the multiplier to reverse a change belongs to the reverse-problems group. Both tiers. (R9)

subtopics.title: Reading a multiplier
subtopics.description: Recovering the change a multiplier applies, where ×0.88 hides a 12% fall.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover decoding multipliers back to percentage changes: x1.045 as a 4.5% rise, x0.88 as a 12% fall, x2.3 as a 130% increase, including factors above 2 and changes over 100%. Also read the combined multiplier of a repeated change. Forming multipliers is the sibling pages; model reading continues in Growth and decay. Both tiers. (R9)

subtopics.title: Measuring a change as a percentage
subtopics.description: Dividing the change by the original amount, never the new one, as a percentage.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover percentage change as change divided by original times 100, rises and falls, calculator and simple non-calculator cases, changes beyond 100%, and the dividing-by-the-new-value error. Expressing one quantity as a percentage of another in general is Number's FDP work; profit wording and fair comparisons are the sibling pages. Both tiers. (R9)

subtopics.title: Percentage profit and loss
subtopics.description: Profit or loss as a percentage of the cost price the seller originally paid.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover percentage profit and loss as a percentage of cost price: from cost and selling prices, finding a selling price to achieve a stated percentage profit, and losses handled as decreases. Stress the of-the-cost-price denominator. Recovering a cost price from a selling price is the reverse-problems group's work. Both tiers. (R9)

subtopics.title: Comparing changes by percentage
subtopics.description: Deciding which rise or fall is proportionally larger, whatever the amounts say.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover deciding which of two rises or falls is proportionally larger by computing each percentage change, including cases where the bigger absolute change is the smaller percentage, and comparing two quantities using percentages, like scores out of different totals. Index numbers are beyond GCSE. Multiplier skills come from the sibling group. Both tiers. (R9)

subtopics.title: The original after an increase
subtopics.description: Recovering the pre-increase amount by dividing by the multiplier, as with VAT.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover reverse percentage after an increase: divide the final amount by the increase multiplier to recover the original, with VAT, pay rise and population contexts, plus a re-applying check. Non-calculator cases with 20% and 25%. Decrease versions and classifying forward against reverse are the sibling pages; depreciation over years is Growth and decay. Both tiers. (R9)

subtopics.title: The original after a decrease
subtopics.description: Recovering the full price from a sale price by dividing by the multiplier.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover reverse percentage after a decrease: divide the sale or reduced value by the decrease multiplier, refuting the add-the-percentage-back shortcut with a numeric counterexample. Sale price and depreciated value contexts, single step only. Increases are the sibling page; multi-year decay with powers of the multiplier belongs to Growth and decay. Both tiers. (R9)

subtopics.title: Spotting a reverse problem
subtopics.description: Deciding whether a question states the original amount or the changed one.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover classifying percentage problems before solving: does the question state the original (multiply) or the changed amount (divide)? Mixed forward and reverse sets, increase and decrease, and language cues like 'after the rise' or 'was'. No new arithmetic; techniques come from the multiplier and reverse sibling pages. Both tiers. (R9)

subtopics.title: Simple interest
subtopics.description: Interest paid on the starting amount only, so the same sum is added every year.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover simple interest, named in R9's financial mathematics: the same interest on the principal every year, total interest and final balance after n years, and finding the rate, time or principal from a stated total. Contrast with compounding stays brief here; simple-versus-compound-interest and Growth and decay own it. Both tiers. (R9)

subtopics.title: Repeated percentage change
subtopics.description: Applying the same change repeatedly by raising the multiplier to a power.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover applying one percentage change n times as the multiplier raised to the power n, why adding percentages fails (two 10% rises give 21%, not 20%), and small-n money and population questions. Different consecutive changes are successive-changes; the compound interest formula, depreciation and how-long questions live in Growth and decay. Both tiers. (R9, R16)

subtopics.title: Successive different changes
subtopics.description: Combining two changes into one multiplier; a 20% rise then 20% fall loses money.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover combining two different consecutive changes into one multiplier, x1.2 then x0.8 making x0.96, a 4% loss, reading off the overall change, order irrelevance, and finding a missing second change from the overall effect. Same-change repetition is repeated-change; reversing a combined change uses the reverse-problems methods. Both tiers. (R9)

subtopics.title: Simple versus compound interest
subtopics.description: Why the same rate pays differently under the two schemes, and the widening gap.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover the two interest schemes side by side: same principal and rate tabulated year by year, which pays more, why the gap widens, and exam questions asking for the difference after n years. Calculation methods are assumed from simple-interest and repeated-change; the compound formula and its decay twin live in Growth and decay. Both tiers. (R9, R16)

topics.title: Compound measures
topics.cardDescription: Speed, density and pressure, rates of pay and flow, and gradients as rates.
topics.metaDescription: GCSE compound measures: speed, density, pressure, rates of pay and unit pricing, converting rates, and gradients read as rates of change.

subtopics.title: Speed, distance and time
subtopics.description: Using speed as distance per unit time to find any quantity from the other two.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover speed as distance per unit time, rearranged to find any of the three, units mph, km/h and m/s, and decimal-hour care (2.4 hours is 2 h 24 min). Single-stage journeys only. Multi-stage averages are average-speed, unit switching is converting-rates, and graph readings sit in the rates-on-graphs group. Both tiers. (R11, R1)

subtopics.title: Average speed
subtopics.description: Total distance divided by total time, not an average of the two speeds.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover average speed as total distance over total time across multi-stage journeys including stops, why averaging two speeds fails even over equal distances, and finding a missing stage from a stated overall average. Distance-time graph versions are speed-from-a-distance-time-graph; velocity, acceleration and kinematics formulas are A level mechanics. Both tiers. (R11)

subtopics.title: Density, mass and volume
subtopics.description: Using density as mass per unit volume, with the units naming the formula.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover density as mass per unit volume, rearranged for any quantity, units g/cm3 and kg/m3 with consistency checks, volumes either given or found from Geometry's mensuration formulas. Single materials only here; combining materials is density-of-a-mixture, and rewriting a density in other units belongs to converting-rates. Both tiers. (R11)

subtopics.title: The density of a mixture
subtopics.description: Totalling mass and volume separately, never averaging the two densities.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover mixture density by totalling mass and totalling volume separately then dividing, never averaging the densities, including finding an unknown component's mass or volume from a stated mixture density. Alloy and liquid contexts, ratios of components included. Parts-based mixing without density is Ratio's mixing-and-concentrations. Both tiers, though exam demand is crossover-level. (R11)

subtopics.title: Pressure, force and area
subtopics.description: Using pressure as force per unit area, and why a smaller area raises pressure.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover pressure as force per unit area, rearranged for any of the three, units N/m2, areas sometimes computed from Geometry's formulas, and reasoning about why a smaller contact area raises pressure. Numerical cases only; gas laws and liquid-column pressure are physics, and algebraic rate conversion is the Higher converting-units-with-algebra page. Both tiers. (R11)

subtopics.title: Rates of pay
subtopics.description: Hourly pay as money per unit time, including part hours and overtime rates.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover pay as money per unit time: wages from hourly rates including part hours as decimals or fractions, overtime at time-and-a-half or double, and comparing jobs by converting to a common rate. Multiplicative structure only; percentage deductions such as tax draw on Percentage change pages. Both tiers. (R11, R1)

subtopics.title: Unit pricing
subtopics.description: The price of one unit as a rate, multiplied or divided to cost any amount.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover price per unit as a rate used both ways: multiply to cost a quantity, divide to find what a budget buys, and price-per-100g comparisons. Deliberate overlap with Proportion's best-buy-comparisons: that page owns choosing between packs and offers, this one the rate mechanics and rearrangement. Both tiers. (R11)

subtopics.title: Rates of flow
subtopics.description: Filling and emptying at a stated volume per unit time, and how long it takes.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover flow as volume per unit time at a constant rate: filling or emptying time from container volume and rate, volume delivered in a stated time, litre and cm3 links, minute and second conversions. Constant rates only; depth-time graphs of odd-shaped containers are Algebra's graph work, gradients the rates-on-graphs group's. Both tiers. (R11, R1)

subtopics.title: Converting a rate between units
subtopics.description: Changing a rate such as m/s into km/h, converting top and bottom separately.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover converting a compound rate between unit systems by converting numerator and denominator separately: m/s to km/h, g/cm3 to kg/m3, pence per gram to pounds per kilogram, numeric cases only with the two-step chain shown. Algebraic versions like x m/s are the next page; single-unit conversion mechanics are Number's. Both tiers. (R1, R11)

topics.title: Growth and decay
topics.cardDescription: Compound interest, depreciation, exponential change, and the models behind them.
topics.metaDescription: GCSE growth and decay: compound interest, depreciation, exponential growth and decay, and iterative models, with the mistakes that lose marks.

subtopics.title: Compound interest
subtopics.description: Interest paid on the balance, so each year's interest earns interest itself.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover compound interest year by year: interest earned on the growing balance, tabulating balances over two or three years, and the contrast with simple interest's flat additions. Small n by repeated multiplication only; the one-step power formula is the sibling page. Simple interest itself lives under Percentage change. Both tiers, since R16 does not brace compound interest. (R16, R9)

subtopics.title: The compound interest formula
subtopics.description: Raising the multiplier to the number of years to reach the balance in one step.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover the closed form, final amount equals principal times the multiplier to the power n: identifying principal, rate and n from wordy questions, decimal-rate care (2.5% gives 1.025), and interest earned versus final balance. Finding n belongs to finding-how-long; extracting an unknown rate by nth roots leans Higher and should be flagged as such. Both tiers. (R16, R9)

subtopics.title: Depreciation
subtopics.description: A value falling by a fixed percentage each year, via a multiplier below 1.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover depreciation as repeated percentage loss: a multiplier below 1 raised to the power n for cars and equipment, final value and total loss, and mixed questions where the rate changes between years so different factors multiply. One-step reverse (original value) problems belong to Percentage change's reverse pages. Both tiers. (R16, R9)

subtopics.title: Finding how long growth takes
subtopics.description: Multiplying period by period until a target is passed, counting whole periods.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover finding how many periods growth or decay needs to pass a target: multiply period by period or trial powers, answer as a whole number of periods, and justify by showing the balances either side of the target. Include decay dropping below a threshold. Logarithms are A level and must not appear. Both tiers. (R16)

subtopics.title: Exponential growth
subtopics.description: Quantities multiplied by the same factor each period, slowly then very fast.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover exponential growth beyond money, populations, bacteria doubling and chain effects, modelled as start times multiplier to the power n, evaluating for given n, building the multiplier from a percentage rate or a doubling description, and comparing growth across equal periods. Curve recognition stays informal; plotting exponential graphs is Algebra's Higher content. Both tiers. (R16)

subtopics.title: Exponential decay
subtopics.description: Repeated multiplication by a factor below 1, never quite reaching zero.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover exponential decay: repeated multiplication by a factor below 1 for radioactivity-style, medicine-dose and cooling contexts, halving as x0.5 per period, and why values approach zero without reaching it. Keep half-life language informal. Threshold questions belong to finding-how-long; the decay curve is sketch-recognition only, with plotting in Algebra at Higher. Both tiers. (R16)

subtopics.title: Linear versus exponential growth
subtopics.description: Adding the same amount against multiplying by the same factor, and which wins.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover the contrast between adding a fixed amount per period and multiplying by a fixed factor: side-by-side tables, which savings account or population overtakes and roughly when, and identifying the model from a description or table. Connects simple-versus-compound-interest with Algebra's arithmetic and geometric sequences; sequence notation stays out. Both tiers. (R16)

subtopics.title: Setting up an exponential model
subtopics.description: Writing repeated change as a starting value times a multiplier to the power n.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover translating a description of repeated change into start times multiplier to the power n: identify the starting value, turn the rate or factor into a multiplier, define what n counts, and state the model before evaluating. Growth and decay both. Interpreting a given model is the sibling page; subscripted recurrence rules are Higher's iterative-processes. Both tiers. (R16)

subtopics.title: Interpreting an exponential model
subtopics.description: Reading a model's starting value and rate, and where it stops being realistic.
subtopics.coverNote: Cover reading a supplied model such as V = 12000 x 0.85 to the power n: state the initial value, decode the multiplier into a percentage change per period, evaluate at a given n, and criticise long-term realism. Multiplier decoding is taught at reading-a-multiplier under Percentage change; building models is the sibling page. Both tiers. (R16, R9)

subtopics.title: General iterative processes
subtopics.description: Applying a stated rule repeatedly, each term built from the one before.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only, from R16's braced clause. Cover applying a stated rule repeatedly with subscript notation: given a start and a term-to-term rule, generate terms, model stock-with-removal situations, and describe long-term behaviour informally. Iteration for solving equations, x = g(x) with rearrangement, is Algebra's A20 territory, not this page's. (R16)

subtopics.title: Growth with regular payments
subtopics.description: A fixed amount added each period before interest, so no single formula works.
subtopics.coverNote: Higher only. Cover accounts with a fixed deposit or withdrawal each period alongside percentage interest: build the balance step by step in the order the question states, over two to four periods, and show why no single power formula applies. Plain compound interest is the both-tier opening pages; annuity formulas are beyond GCSE. (R16, R9)
